newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori renews vow to seek bloodless siege outcome.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori renews vow to seek bloodless siege outcome.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori renewed his pledge to find a negotiated settlement to Peru's 110-day hostage crisis, saying he would intervene with force only as a last resort in an "uncontrollable emergency."

With the siege at the Japanese ambassador's house dragging into its 16th week, Fujimori returned to Lima from Bolivia late on Saturday with words of support from his Bolivian counterpart Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada and a vow to keep negotiating.

"We are not contemplating the use of force. The use of force is a move which would become the last (resort), useful in an uncontrollable emergency which we hope will not occur," Fujimori told a news conference in the Bolivian city of Santa Cruz.
"We will continue exhausting all efforts ... to reach a peaceful outcome," said Fujimori, admitting he had no idea when that might be.

The "uncontrollable emergency" appeared to be a reference to the possibility of violence by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) against the 72 hostages -- a scenario Fujimori has said could bring swift military intervention.
There was no sign the MRTA had physically harmed any hostages, although many are reported to be suffering stress-related disorders after months in captivity.

The lack of progress in talks to end the siege has strengthened the hand of people in Fujimori's government who want to use force, news reports have said. But Japan, which legally would have to approve any armed incursion into its diplomatic compound, has insisted on a peaceful solution.

About 20 MRTA rebels stormed the residence during a cocktail party on Dec. 17 and took some 500 guests hostage, later releasing all but a VIP list of 72 people including two cabinet ministers, Fujimori's brother and the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia.
Speculation was rife in Lima on Sunday that one of the crisis mediators had taken negotiations directly to the hostage-takers' leadership.

Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani, a member of a three-man mediation team, visited a naval base in the port of Callao where the MRTA's maximum leader Victor Polay and at least two other MRTA prisoners are serving life sentences.

News reports said Cipriani spoke to Polay during the hour-long visit to the prison on Friday evening. Cipriani was silent about the visit, but MRTA made a reference to the base in a poster hung from a residence window early on Sunday. The poster said, "Down with the jail-tombs of the Callao naval base."
Fujimori told reporters he had not talked to Cipriani about the visit but would be in contact with him soon after arriving in Lima.
Local newspapers speculated on Saturday that Cipriani hoped Polay would persuade Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, leader of the MRTA guerrillas holed up in the diplomatic compound, to give up his struggle.
Fujimori's government has not met the hostage-takers for face-to-face talks since mid-March, leaving the mediation panel to carry out a kind of shuttle diplomacy between the two sides.
Talks appear to have stalled on the issue of the MRTA's demands for freedom for about 450 jailed comrades, including Polay, in exchange for release of the hostages.

The mediation team consisting of Cipriani, Red Cross mbassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross representative Michel Minnig entered the besieged residence for about an hour on Saturday, with no comment afterward. Cipriani later went to the home of chief government negotiator Domingo Palermo for two more hours.
